answers.text: Every driver's text reads a bit differently, so I would say: reply with exactly three lines, same order every time — drop-off time, pallet count, then any damage noted, and if one of those is not mentioned in the message, write 'not stated' rather than leaving it blank. That way the log always has three lines to read.
For the call log, I would say: list each entry with time, customer, topic, outcome, in that order.

Something about the finishing time in this note is off — access from 8am plus six hours should not really stretch to finishing the next day. I would want someone to look at it again before it is filed.
118 up from 96 does not really work out to 20% — it is closer to 23%, so that is what I would flag first. I did not look closely at the balance figures.
I would sign off Output 2, since it gives the real numbers behind the 88%, 827 out of 940. Output 1 does not show where its figure comes from.

I would send Email 2, since the volume numbers, 1,200 to 1,650, back up the tier-2 claim. Email 1 is not necessarily wrong, but 'we'd expect better' on its own cannot be checked against anything — once someone had the numbers behind it, it could probably go out fine too.

1. No, keep the pricing internal for now. 2. Yes, that is just a total. 3. No, that budget has not been signed off. 4. I would probably leave that one out too, just to be safe. 5. No, that is a home address.

The rates and retainer cap I would treat carefully, and the non-disclosure clause too since it names both sides. The general service scope I would be fine to paste in as it is, since there is nothing about money or names in it.

Before it goes to the manager at month end, I would check the closing stock figure against the warehouse system as a fixed step — that is the kind of check that would actually catch a wrong total, not just a typo in the write-up.
Step 1 is the one I would watch, since a misread invoice number at the start would carry through the rest.
